Argentine Rail Blockade Ends, Businesses Resume Operations After Political Unrest

Buenos Aires—Economic activity across Argentina is returning to normal this week following the resolution of a nationwide rail blockade that brought freight and passenger transport to a near standstill for over ten days. The blockade, sparked by political unrest over proposed constitutional reforms, disrupted supply chains, halted exports, and forced major companies including Pluspetrol SA to temporarily suspend or scale back operations.

The crisis began on May 28, when unions and social groups, joined by provincial leaders critical of President Jimena Torres’s government, blocked key railway lines in protest of sweeping judicial changes set to be voted on in Congress. The protests escalated, with demonstrators occupying stations and rail yards from Rosario to Neuquén, and clashed with federal police in several locations. The resulting paralysis left farms unable to move harvests, factories short of inputs, and energy firms struggling to deliver fuel.

Pluspetrol SA, a major energy producer, confirmed that operations at its Neuquén basin gas facilities slowed to minimum capacity as a result of the blockade. “Our supply chain depends on reliable transport. The rail disruption forced us to curtail activity to ensure safety and manage inventories,” said a company spokesperson. The Argentine Chamber of Commerce estimated the economic losses from the blockade at over $340 million, with logistics costs rising sharply.

After days of tense negotiations brokered by the Catholic Church and international mediators, the government and opposition agreed late Sunday to delay the judicial reforms and initiate a national dialogue. By Monday morning, rail union leaders announced the end of the blockade and called for calm. Trains resumed service by midday across most of the country.

Transport Minister Carla Ríos praised the compromise, saying, “Argentina’s economy cannot afford paralysis. We thank all sides for putting the country first.” Analysts welcomed the resolution but warned that underlying political divisions remain. “It’s a reprieve, not a solution. The economic impact will linger, particularly for exporters,” said analyst Martín Velasco.

Pluspetrol SA and other affected companies reported on Wednesday that normal operations had resumed. The government pledged to assess compensation mechanisms for companies and workers hit by the disruption. Markets reacted positively, with the peso gaining 2% against the dollar by midday.
